seo.title: The Linux Command That Wipes A Disk In 4 Characters
seo.hook: No prompt. No undo. Four characters.
seo.description: dd copies raw blocks and asks nothing of anybody. One wrong letter overwrites your running system.

scenes.narration: Somewhere on every beginner's Linux list is a command that wipes a whole disk in four characters. Which one?

That command is D D. It copies raw blocks, and it asks nothing of anybody. Two arguments do all the work: I F equals is the input, the thing you read from, and O F equals is the output, the thing you write over. Used properly it's excellent. Read your disk, write a file, and that's a genuine full backup. Read the file back onto a spare disk and you've restored it. Now swap one letter so the output is slash dev slash S D A, and that's your running system being overwritten while you watch. No prompt, no progress bar, no undo. Four characters. Add status equals progress so it at least tells you what it's doing. Read the of= argument twice, out loud, before you press return. Every single time.

cmdDd.headline: dd is the [four characters]

steps.label: dd if=/dev/sda of=backup.img
steps.detail: reads the whole disk into a file

steps.label: dd if=backup.img of=/dev/sda
steps.detail: one letter wrong. that is the running system.

cmdDd.verdict: Four characters, and the disk is gone
